extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics instructors / course designers using projects, portfolios, and writing for assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rubrics for assessing student learning in undergraduate mathematics courses, especially project reports, group work, portfolios, and writing assignments. Includes analytic and holistic scoring scales, portfolio requirements, and practical implementation tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding (analytic scale)
rubrics_metrics.description:
3 Pts: The student(s) demonstrates a complete understanding of the problem in the problem statement section as well as in the development of the plan and interpretation of the solution.
2 Pts: The student(s) demonstrates a good understanding of the problem in the problem statement section. Some minor point(s) of the problem may be overlooked in the problem statement, the development of the plan, or the interpretation of the solution.
1 Pt: The student(s) demonstrates minimal understanding of the problem. The problem statement may be unclear to the reader. The plan and/or interpretation of the solution overlooks significant parts of the problem.
0 Pt: The student(s) demonstrates no understanding of the problem. The problem statement section does not address the problem or may even be missing. The plan and discussion of the solution have nothing to do with the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one dimension of an analytic scale for project reports (sample adapted from [1]). Use point levels 0–3 to discriminate degrees of comprehension shown in problem statement, plan development, and solution interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan (analytic scale)
rubrics_metrics.description:
3 Pts: The plan is clearly articulated AND will lead to a correct solution.
2 Pts: The plan is articulated reasonably well and correct OR may contain a minor flaw based on a correct interpretation of the problem.
1 Pt: The plan is not clearly presented OR only partially correct based on a correct/partially correct understanding of the problem.
0 Pt: There is no plan OR the plan is completely incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score plans on clarity and whether the plan (as stated) will lead to a correct solution. Distinguish minor flaws (2 pts) from major or absent plans (1 or 0 pts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Solution (analytic scale)
rubrics_metrics.description:
3 Pts: The solution is correct AND clearly labeled OR though the solution is incorrect it is the expected outcome of a slightly flawed plan that is correctly implemented.
2 Pts: Solution is incorrect due to a minor error in implementation of either a correct or incorrect plan OR solution is not clearly labeled.
1 Pt: Solution is incorrect due to a significant error in implementation of either a correct or incorrect plan.
0 Pt: No solution is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both correctness and whether the solution follows from the plan implemented. Labeling and minor algebraic/implementation errors are distinguished from significant errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation (analytic scale)
rubrics_metrics.description:
1 Pt: Overall appearance of the paper is neat and easy to read. All pertinent information can be readily found.
0 Pt: Paper is hard to read OR pertinent information is hard to find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A binary (0/1) rubric for readable, well-organized presentation and accessibility of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scoring: 4 Points — Exemplary Response
rubrics_metrics.description: All of the following characteristics must be present: • The answer is correct. • The explanation is clear and complete. • The explanation includes complete implementation of a mathematically correct plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holistic top score requires correctness, clarity, and full implementation of a correct plan. Use holistic judgments when an overall single score is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scoring: 3 Points — Good Response
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly one of the following characteristics is present: a The answer is incorrect due to a minor flaw in plan or an algebraic error. b The explanation lacks clarity. c The explanation is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using letters (e.g., '3a') indicate which of the three characteristics is lacking — students value this feedback. Use for quick overall grading when analytic detail is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scoring: 2 Points — Inadequate Response
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly two of the characteristics in the 3-point section are present OR One or more of the following characteristics are present: a The answer is incorrect due to a major flaw in the plan. b The explanation lacks clarity or is incomplete but does indicate some correct and relevant reasoning. c A plan is partially implemented and no solution is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 2 points for responses with multiple deficiencies or a major flaw in approach; captures partial understanding or incomplete implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scoring: 1 Point — Poor Response
rubrics_metrics.description: All of the following characteristics must be present: • The answer is incorrect. • The explanation, if any, uses irrelevant arguments. • No plan for solution is attempted beyond just copying data given in the problem statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowest passing-level holistic score reserved for responses showing irrelevant reasoning and no genuine attempt to plan a solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scoring: 0 Points — No Response
rubrics_metrics.description: The student’s paper is blank or contains only work that appears to have no relevance to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 0 for blank or totally irrelevant submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scale development guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When new scales are developed it is well worth remembering that as the number of points increases so does the difficulty in developing and applying the scale. In the case of the holistic scale, it is often best to start with four points. As you gain experience, you may decide to develop more detailed scales. I have always found five or at most six points sufficient for holistic scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: begin with ~4-point holistic scales; more points increase rater difficulty. Use letters to indicate which characteristic is lacking (e.g., '3a').

rubrics_metrics.name: Group project contribution logging and weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid problems with one or two students in a group doing all of the work, have students log the hours spent on the project. Warn the class that if a student in a group spends 20 minutes on the project while each of the other members averages four hours, that person will receive one-twelfth of the total grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time logs and pre-specified proportional grade adjustments to deter free-riding. Track contributions and apply clear penalties when logs show gross imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio defining features
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolios are concrete and somewhat personal expressions of growth and development. The following elements, abstracted from artist portfolios, are common to all portfolios and, taken together, distinguish them from other assessment tools: • work of high quality, • accumulated over time, • chosen (in part) by the student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three features to decide whether an assessment artifact qualifies as a portfolio and whether portfolio assessment is appropriate for given goals (documenting growth, student choice, quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective portfolio assignment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Select three pieces of work from this semester to include in your portfolio. The purpose is to highlight your selections and give an analysis in your own words. The instructor will focus on two things: (1) an understanding of some key concepts in [course] and (2) a self-awareness of your journey (where you started from, where you went, and where you are now). Your analysis should explain your reasons for picking these pieces. Write more than one paragraph but no more than five pages. The portfolio is 5% of your final grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grade reflective portfolios on demonstrated understanding of key concepts and the student's reflective self-awareness. Limit length (1+ paragraphs to 5 pages) and require explicit rationale for selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project portfolio — required report elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Project reports must include: a cover page with a title, author’s name, and an abstract; clear statements of problems solved, along with their solutions; a discussion of what was learned and its relevance to the course; acknowledgement of any assistance; and a list of references. Reports are usually between five and ten pages long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reports on both mathematical content and quality of presentation. Use first and final drafts (especially early in course) and require standard components (title/abstract/problems/solutions/discussion/acknowledgements/references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Project portfolio logistics and process guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For the typical project, students will have one week to produce a first draft and another week to complete the final draft. Students may be working on two different projects in different stages at the same time. Allowing for test breaks and longer projects, a completed course portfolio will comprise seven to ten projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require drafts, use peer review, conferences, and compiled feedback sheets to streamline grading. Share examples of good work to communicate expectations. Expect students to need several projects to understand thoroughness and clarity required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective portfolio / journal practice
rubrics_metrics.description: To increase students’ self-awareness of how their understanding has developed, require information collected by students during the course. Keeping a journal for the course is useful: e.g., make a journal entry two or three times each week reflecting on readings or problem sets, difficulties or successes, clarifying or connecting concepts, or feelings toward the course. The teacher collects and responds to the journals on a regular basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regular teacher feedback on journals; cycle through all journals every few weeks as an efficient reading schedule. Journals feed into end-of-semester reflective portfolios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project assignment content expectations (example: Vector Spaces of Polynomials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect students to: state properties defining the structure (e.g., vector space), show P3 is a vector space with natural definitions, find a basis for P3 and coordinate representations, show differentiation is a linear transformation P3→P2, find matrix representations relative to chosen bases, check work by comparing matrix action with derivative, and discuss what was learned and whether the project changed their thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a discussion section asking what was learned and how the project influenced conceptual understanding. This explicit reflective discussion is part of the grading rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading priorities for mathematics writing assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: When grading writing assignments, the instructor's primary concern is accuracy and secondary concern is organization. Creativity and originality are not required but may be voluntarily included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight correctness of mathematical content above stylistic or creative elements; indicate expectations to students (accuracy first, then organization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph analysis assignment requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Find or create a graph representing a real-world situation that exhibits at least six aspects from the class-compiled list of graph aspects. Make a chart indicating each aspect of the graph, where it occurs, and what it indicates about the function or its derivatives. Then write a narrative explaining connections between each graph aspect and the real-world situation it represents. Final paper must include the graph, the chart, and the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assignment assesses conceptual transfer (applying course ideas to real situations). Instructor explicitly is not evaluating computational ability here, but critical/analytical/interpretive skills. Allow ~3 weeks; specify audience when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann sums paper — audience and format guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Riemann sum paper, specify the audience that the students should address (usually someone with minimal exposure to mathematics such as a younger sibling). Students are given at least three weeks to complete each writing assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying an audience helps students practice explanatory writing and assess conceptual understanding rather than computation. Allow substantial time for drafts and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of portfolio findings to inform teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflective portfolios and project drafts can reveal student difficulties and inform real-time teaching adjustments (e.g., re-teach concepts, reorganize topic order) and future course redesign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat portfolios as formative data: use journals and drafts to identify widespread misunderstandings and adjust instruction mid-course or in future iterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success factors & practical tips for portfolio and writing assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflective and project portfolios are writing-intensive; clarity, time, and patience are required of teachers and students. Techniques: compile common comments on feedback sheets, use peer review, hold conferences, share exemplary student work, and cycle journal reading every few weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operational guidelines reduce instructor workload and improve student outcomes; expect variability in student comfort with reflective writing and allow for a range of reflections.
